intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Stickler syndrome type VI (STL6) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the COL9A3 gene (120270) on chromosome 20q13.33.

checks.claim: Stickler syndrome type VI (STL6) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the COL9A3 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: 19 patients have been reported (Baker et al., 2011; Faletra et al., 2014; Hanson‐Kahn et al., 2018; Nikopoulos et al., 2011; Nixon et al., 2019) with STL caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in genes encoding for the three chains of type IX collagen.
checks.explanation: The paper describes recessive STL caused by homozygous mutations and, in its own case, compound heterozygous mutations in COL9A3. The STL6 label is standard nomenclature.

checks.evidence_quote: homozygosity for a loss of function mutation in COL9A3, which encodes the α3 chain of type IX procollagen
checks.explanation: The chromosomal location is standard nomenclature added to the gene name; the paper itself does not state it.

paragraphs.text: Stickler syndrome type VI is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in COL9A3. In a review of 7 families, Rad et al. (2022) found that consistent features were moderate-to-profound progressive sensorineural hearing loss and moderate to high myopia with vitreoretinal degeneration. Retinal detachment and cataract occurred occasionally, and skeletal involvement was more variable. Markova et al. (2021) noted that none of the patients they reviewed had cleft palate.

checks.claim: Stickler syndrome type VI is an autosomal recessive disorder.
checks.evidence_quote: Here, we report a new case of a patient with recessive Stickler syndrome caused by novel compound heterozygous mutations in the COL9A3 gene with a more severe phenotype.
checks.explanation: The paper describes COL9A3-related STL as recessive.

checks.claim: Stickler syndrome type VI is caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in COL9A3.
checks.evidence_quote: To date only three clinical descriptions of six patients from three families with homozygous mutations in this gene are available. All the described mutations have led to the loss of function (LoF).
checks.explanation: The previously reported variants were homozygous LoF, and the new case had compound heterozygous LoF variants. Together these are biallelic LoF variants.

checks.claim: Rad et al. (2022) reviewed 7 families with Stickler syndrome type VI.
checks.evidence_quote: Our report re-affirms previous studies that have described four families with biallelic LOF causing autosomal recessive STL, increasing the total number of families reported to date to seven.
checks.explanation: Four previous families plus the paper's three make seven.

checks.claim: In the 7 families with Stickler syndrome type VI reviewed by Rad et al. (2022), moderate-to-profound progressive sensorineural hearing loss was a consistent feature.
checks.evidence_quote: Consistent clinical features among STL patients with biallelic COL9A3 LOF alleles comprise moderate-to-profound progressive sensorineural hearing loss and moderate high myopia with vitreoretinal degeneration.
checks.explanation: The paper names this hearing loss as a consistent feature.

paragraphs.text: Hanson-Kahn et al. (2018) reported a boy with autosomal recessive Stickler syndrome, born to consanguineous parents (third cousins) from India. He failed newborn hearing screening. At 5 months he had moderate to severe sensorineural hearing loss on the right and severe loss on the left, which remained stable. Temporal bone CT showed mild enlargement of the vestibular aqueducts. He had no myopia at 5 months. By 2 years he had myopia of -6.75 OD and -8 OS, which progressed to -10.75 OD and -11.25 OS by 12 years. He had no vitreous abnormalities. Femoral and tibial bowing were present at birth. Radiographs at 6 years showed slightly flattened proximal femoral epiphyses, flattened acetabula, irregularity of the medial distal femoral epiphyses, and mild platyspondyly. He also had midface hypoplasia and did not have cleft palate. Growth and intelligence were normal. Autoimmune hypothyroidism was diagnosed at 10 years.

One family (1 patient) had a COL9A1 variant, 2 families (3 patients) had COL9A2 variants, and 1 family (2 patients) had a COL9A3 variant. All patients were highly myopic, with congenital megalophthalmos and abnormal, hypoplastic vitreous gel, and all had sensorineural hearing loss. One patient had severe arthropathy.

paragraphs.text: Markova et al. (2021) reported a boy with autosomal recessive Stickler syndrome, born to healthy nonconsanguineous Russian parents. At 1 month he had hip dysplasia with bilateral absence of ossification centers. At 3 months he had congenital high bilateral myopia. At 11 months he was diagnosed with bilateral grade 3-4 sensorineural hearing loss, and he had delayed speech. Radiographs at 1 and 3 years showed mild spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia with spina bifida occulta of the sacral vertebrae, mild platyspondyly, kyphosis, flattened and irregular femoral heads, coxa valga, and flattened distal femoral epiphyses. Eye examination showed peripheral pigment changes, multiple vitreous floaters, and a preretinal membrane, and the ERG was normal. At age 2 years 5 months he had genu valgum, waddling gait, lower limb joint pain, a flat nasal bridge, mild midface hypoplasia, and a high palate, without cleft palate. The authors considered his joint pain from age 3 years to be early-onset arthropathy.
